summary.text: Velocity measures how fast an object moves along with the specific direction of its motion.
Instantaneous velocity represents the speed and direction an object would maintain if its acceleration stopped at that exact moment.
On a displacement-time graph, instantaneous velocity is represented by the slope of the line tangent to the curve at any single point.

items.prompt: Imagine a train traveling around a circular track at a steady 50 km/h. Why is it considered to be accelerating?

options.label: Its speed is constantly increasing as it turns.
Its direction of motion is constantly changing.
Its total distance traveled decreases with every turn.
Its frame of reference is at rest.

items.explain: An object undergoes acceleration if its speed, direction, or both change. Moving in a curve changes direction continuously even at a steady speed.

items.prompt: A runner looks at a graph of their position over time. How can they determine their instantaneous velocity at a specific second?

options.label: By measuring the slope of the tangent line touching the curve at that point.
By calculating the total area underneath the curve up to that second.
By finding the slope of a secant line between the start and finish points.
By dividing the total distance traveled by the elapsed time.

items.explain: On a displacement-time graph, instantaneous velocity corresponds to the slope of the line tangent to the curve at that precise point.

items.prompt: How does instantaneous velocity differ from average velocity on a displacement-time graph?

options.label: Instantaneous velocity uses distance, while average velocity uses acceleration.
Instantaneous velocity is represented by the area under the curve.
Average velocity is the slope of a secant line, while instantaneous velocity uses a tangent line.
Average velocity is always greater than speed, whereas instantaneous velocity is lower.

items.explain: Average velocity is given by the slope of a secant line connecting two boundary points, while instantaneous velocity is the slope of a tangent line at one point.

items.prompt: If a moving object suddenly stops accelerating right now, what motion will it maintain from this moment forward?

options.label: The average velocity calculated across its entire past journey.
The escape speed required to leave Earth's gravitational pull.
Zero velocity, coming to an immediate complete stop.
The instantaneous velocity it possessed at that exact moment.

items.explain: Instantaneous velocity can be understood as the velocity an object would continue traveling at if it stopped accelerating at that moment.

items.prompt: Why is the term 'escape velocity' technically inaccurate when describing leaving Earth?

options.label: Because it only applies to objects rotating counter-clockwise.
Because achieving 11,200 m/s works regardless of the direction traveled.
Because it changes depending on whether relativity applies.
Because velocity cannot be measured in metres per second.

items.explain: It is more accurately an escape speed because reaching that speed magnitude allows an object to break free regardless of direction, as long as it hits nothing.

items.prompt: Under classical Newtonian mechanics, how do non-accelerating observers describe an object's acceleration?

options.label: They each calculate different acceleration values depending on reference frame.
They disagree on elapsed time, altering their acceleration measurements.
They all calculate and agree on the exact same acceleration values.
They can only measure relative position, not acceleration.

items.explain: In Newtonian mechanics, all observers agree on time, so non-accelerating observers describe an object's acceleration using identical values.

paragraphs.heading: Velocity at a moment
paragraphs.text: Velocity says how fast an object moves and in which direction. It is a basic idea in kinematics, the part of mechanics that describes how objects move. It is a vector, meaning it needs both a size and a direction to define it. Instantaneous velocity is often just called velocity.

paragraphs.heading: A way to picture it
paragraphs.text: The idea of a velocity at a single instant can feel strange at first. One helpful picture is this: the instantaneous velocity is the velocity the object would carry on with if it stopped accelerating at that moment.

paragraphs.heading: The slope of a tangent
paragraphs.text: On a graph of position against time, the instantaneous velocity at any point is the slope of the tangent line to the curve there. Average velocity is different: it is the slope of a secant line joining the points at the start and end of a time period. That average equals the change in position divided by the time taken, v̄ = Δs/Δt.

paragraphs.heading: A rate of change
paragraphs.text: Velocity is defined as the rate at which position changes. In calculus terms it is the derivative of position with respect to time. That gives a change in metres divided by a change in seconds, so velocity is measured in metres per second. Its size on its own is called speed.

paragraphs.heading: Linking to acceleration
paragraphs.text: Acceleration works the same way one step up. On a graph of velocity against time, the acceleration at a given instant is the slope of the tangent line there, written 𝒂 = d𝒗/dt. In practice it is common to start from an expression for acceleration instead. When the acceleration is constant, 𝒗 = 𝒖 + 𝒂t, where u is the velocity at time t = 0.

paragraphs.heading: Turning counts too
paragraphs.text: Because velocity includes direction, it can change while speed stays the same. Any change in speed, direction or both is acceleration. A car going round a circle at a steady 20 kilometres per hour keeps its speed, but its direction keeps changing, so it is accelerating.
